title: Fourier Transform-Based Computation of Two-Electron Four-Center Coulomb Repulsion Integrals
summary: We present a Fourier-based method for evaluating two-electron four-center Coulomb repulsion integrals over Slater-type orbitals. Spherical Fourier-Bessel coefficients of the convolution factors are precomputed and reused. Since the spherical part of the integral can be evaluated directly, there remains only a one-dimensional quadrature problem in the radial direction. For the ten reference integrals reported here, the largest absolute discrepancy is $1.7\times10^{-9}$. A preliminary resident-cache benchmark computes approximately $4.2\times10^5$ unique integrals per second on an NVIDIA V100 at the contraction stage.

title: Median randomized quasi-Monte Carlo for nested integration
summary: Nested integrals $\int f\left(\int g(\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{x})\mathrm{d}{}\boldsymbol{x}\right)\mathrm{d}{}\boldsymbol{y}$ where $\boldsymbol{y}\in[0,1]^{d_1}$ and $\boldsymbol{x}\in[0,1]^{d_2}$ frequently arise in Bayesian experimental design, medical decision making, and computational finance. Statistical estimators for nested integrals are more computationally demanding than for standard integrals. Recent studies demonstrate that the median randomized quasi-Monte Carlo (mRQMC) method achieves super-polynomial convergence rates for analytic integrands. We extend mRQMC methods to nested integrations and propose a novel double-loop mRQMC estimator with super-polynomial convergence rate if both the inner and outer integrands are analytic. Established estimators for nested integrals, such as double-loop or multilevel Monte Carlo, are by contrast limited to algebraic convergence rates. However, expected information gain (EIG) applications from experimental design typically do not fulfill this condition due to a lack of regularity in the outer integrand. We address this through a theoretically-grounded importance sampling regularization scheme. Although super-polynomial convergence rates remain achievable for the inner integral, only the algebraic rate $α+3/2-ε$ for any $ε>0$ can be theoretically guaranteed for the outer integral in the EIG, where $α\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$ denotes the order of the mixed derivatives of the regularized outer integrand. Our approach shows substantial improvements over double-loop randomized quasi-Monte Carlo methods based on the sample mean in moderately high-dimensional settings for a simple polynomial example. Moreover, we demonstrate improved convergence behavior of the median-based estimator for the more challenging setting of EIG estimation.

title: Variational neural transport for aggregation-diffusion equations
summary: We develop a neural transport framework for nonlinear, nonlocal aggregationdiffusion equations arising in chemotaxis, polymer dynamics, and related applications. Based on the Onsager variational principle, we reformulate the governing equation as a constrained optimal control problem, taking the velocity field as the control and evolving the density via the associated continuity equation. The velocity field is parameterized by a neural network trained on the variational objective evaluated along particle trajectories. By coupling the density and generalized score equations into a single system solved via the Euler method, the score function propagates efficiently for loss evaluation. Furthermore, we establish a rigorous error analysis that decomposes the total error into approximation, optimization, Monte Carlo sampling, and time-discretization components, and prove corresponding error bounds. Numerical experiments across several representative models demonstrate the accuracy and effectiveness of the proposed approach.

title: A kernel-independent precorrected-FFT method
summary: The precorrected-FFT has been used to rapidly evaluate $N$-body sums arising in electromagnetics and acoustics settings. It has, however, been historically limited to kernels that satisfy a Green's identity. In this work, we demonstrate that, using an improved version of the method of proxy points, the precorrected-FFT can be used to efficiently compute $N$-body sums with a wide variety of kernels. This algorithm requires no analytic information beyond pointwise access to the kernel. Our examples include kernels from non-local PDEs, Matern kernels, anisotropic kernels, and the Green's functions of high order PDEs. We also provide a detailed algorithm for choosing the proxy points and spreading grid, as implemented in the new pcfft package. We show these algorithmic choices result in favorable scaling when compared to other kernel-independent fast summation methods. Finally, we use the algorithm to accelerate a wide variety of integral equations solvers involving non-standard kernels, with applications in surface scattering, geophysics, and microbial community formation.

title: Implementation and verification of a new free boundary module for Resistive Wall Modes simulations with the nonlinear 3D full MHD code SpeCyl
summary:
Self-consistent numerical simulations of free boundary instabilities, such as resistive wall modes (RWMs) and external kink modes, require special attention given their relevance on the path towards magnetic fusion based nuclear reactors. In this work, a new implementation and a verification benchmark are presented for the nonlinear three-dimensional (3D) full magneto-hydrodynamics (MHD) code SpeCyl, which self-consistently combines a free flow 3D treatment for the edge plasma velocity with double resistive wall thin shell magnetic boundary conditions, capable of capturing the essential features of common setups in experimental devices. Two coaxial resistive shells surround the plasma. Vacuum conditions are assumed between and outside the resistive shells, whose relative positions and time constants can be varied on purpose.
  The implementation is extensively verified against Shafranov's analytic theory, valid for a circular cross section large aspect ratio tokamak and assuming a flat current profile. The correctness of newly implemented Boundary Conditions (BCs) is confirmed by the good agreement obtained for the linear growth rates of (m=2,n=1) RWM and external kink, over a wide range of wall positions, resistive shell time constants, and for different initial reference equilibria. The (m=2,n=1) RWM growth rates are also benchmarked against previous different RWMs modelling and successful validation studies for RFX-mod tokamak plasmas. The new BCs make SpeCyl a flexible and robust tool to investigate free boundary MHD modes in large aspect ratio magnetic confinement configurations, such as those achieved with the RFX-mod machine and expected in RFX-mod2.

title: Parallel Design of a GPU-Resident Semi-Lagrangian Drift-Kinetic Solver on Unstructured Extruded Tokamak Meshes
summary: Semi-Lagrangian (SL) schemes advect a distribution function along characteristics and remap it to a fixed grid. They are unconditionally stable without a global solve, and with discontinuous Galerkin (DG) integration the transfer along a magnetic field line conserves mass exactly. This paper presents the parallel and GPU design of a 3X+2V SLDG drift-kinetic tokamak solver on unstructured, flux-surface-aligned poloidal planes of shaped cross section, extruded toroidally. Transport follows magnetic field lines across the planes, and each velocity channel advances a fixed distance per step, proportional to its parallel speed, so the halo depth a channel needs grows with its speed. Velocity-dependent ragged halos exploit this, sending each channel only its own upwind depth. The 4D decomposition includes the toroidal angle, the 2D poloidal plane and the magnetic moment, and leaves the parallel velocity whole: no stage transports across the magnetic moment, while a parallel-velocity partition would put a halo inside the acceleration stage. On NVIDIA A100s the design strong-scales over the magnetic-moment axis from one to 12 four-GPU nodes, and a weak series of three points refining all five phase-space dimensions together, 16x in total per series point, holds a weak-scaling efficiency of 75% on 16 GPUs and 57% on 256, from a one-GPU base case. The pointwise interpolations within the poloidal plane do not conserve mass, and the full step's mass drift stays below 2.1x10^-5 at every series point. The design was implemented with an AI code assistant under a machine-checked regression discipline, in which every change is held to one of four exactness classes, from bit-identical to a physics rate within a stated tolerance.

title: Removing Boundary Smoothness from the Hot-Spots Conclusion in the Simple-Eigenvalue Case
summary: We give a reduction from a smooth-domain theorem excluding interior critical points of first positive Neumann eigenfunctions to a non-strict hot-spots conclusion on arbitrary bounded simply connected planar domains with compact Neumann resolvent and simple first positive eigenvalue. The main analytic step is spectral convergence under exhaustion by conformal images of concentric disks. A reflection extension, conformal invariance of Dirichlet energy, and compactness of the Sobolev embedding give a direct proof. A truncation argument justifies square integrability of the transferred extensions without any boundary regularity. The smooth-domain theorem proved by OpenAI is an external input; the approximation argument is proved here in full. The paper was generated by ChatGPT with prompts from the listed author.

title: Riemannian Hessian analysis of Sobolev gradient flows for the Gross--Pitaevskii ground state problem
summary: Sobolev gradient flows for the Gross--Pitaevskii ground state problem are Riemannian gradient descent methods on the sphere under a metric induced by a discrete elliptic operator. We analyze their convergence through the condition number of the Riemannian Hessian at the ground state. Bounds of the Rayleigh quotient of the Riemannian Hessian give a uniform analysis of these methods for different metrics. The uniform analysis applies to the classical metrics, such as the shifted Laplacian and the energy-adaptive metrics. Inspired by this analysis, we also consider three new metrics. One of them is a Thomas--Fermi metric, whose condition number is bounded uniformly in the interaction strength for the one-dimensional harmonic trap and whose iteration count does not grow in the Thomas--Fermi regime in the numerical tests. The performance suggested by our analysis is consistent with three-dimensional numerical tests with up to one billion unknowns, for both Riemannian gradient descent and Riemannian conjugate gradient methods, whose practical performance is also related to the Hessian condition number. The Thomas--Fermi flow needs the fewest iterations, while the metrics inverted exactly by tensor-product solvers are the fastest in computational time on one GPU card.

title: Resistive alignment of a black-hole magnetosphere
summary: Recent numerical simulations have shown that black-hole magnetospheres evolve rapidly toward alignment between the magnetic axis and spin axis but the physical origin of this process has remained unclear. We develop an analytic theory of this alignment within resistive relativistic magnetohydrodynamics. Taking the slow-spin Blandford-Znajek monopole solution as the exterior magnetic field, we reduce the induction equation to a relaxation equation for the current-sheet inclination angle. Our analysis shows that alignment results from second-order spin effects in the Blandford-Znajek solution combined with explicit resistive dissipation. We test this prediction using resistive-GRMHD simulations at several spins and resistivities and find a regime in which the measured late-time secular decay agrees quantitatively with the analytic prediction.

title: Polyconvex neural-network surrogates with learned paired directional features for anisotropic hyperelastic homogenization
summary: Approximating the effective anisotropic hyperelastic response of a representative volume element (RVE) requires constitutive expressiveness, mechanical consistency, and computational efficiency. This work develops a polyconvex physics-augmented neural network (PANN) construction based on paired directional features whose orientations, stretch powers, and determinant exponents adapt to the RVE response. The features are composed with convex, componentwise nondecreasing cores, realized as an input-convex neural network (ICNN) or an input-convex Kolmogorov-Arnold network (ICKAN). The complete energies satisfy objectivity, an exactly stress-free reference, two-dimensional polyconvexity, and prescribed growth conditions by construction, and nonnegative energy is certified separately for the selected models. On a multicavity and a single-cavity periodic cell, these energies are compared with an Unconstrained energy, trained identically without the curvature and growth constraints, and with three hyperreduced projection-based reduced-order models (HPROMs), which serve as physics-based references. On the first cell, learning the features lowers the stress error sevenfold, and six features suffice on both. The constrained energies remain below one percent in stress error and in the displacement error of a tensile-coupon FE$^2$ application with a full-order reference, whereas the Unconstrained energy and the HPROMs are more accurate inside the data. Beyond the data, however, the Unconstrained energy loses rank-one convexity, and under confined compression it stops below half of the 500 MPa that the constrained energies reach. These results quantify what the guarantees cost in accuracy and what they secure beyond the data.

title: A Framework for Arbitrary-Order Electromagnetic Field Approximation Based on Analytical Solutions of Maxwell's Equations
summary: The standard Yee finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) algorithm uses Maxwell's equations to replace first order temporal derivatives with spatial curls. In this work, the relation is extended to arbitrary orders: a Time-Space Theorem establishes the correspondence between higher-order temporal derivatives and successively higher-order spatial curl operators. Based on this relation, an arbitrary-order framework for electromagnetic field approximations is developed. The framework constructs higher temporal orders through higher curl orders and permits different spatial discretizations and curl-estimation techniques, thereby providing a general basis for developing numerical algorithms of arbitrary orders. As one implementation, an arbitrary-order FDTD algorithm is constructed using staggered time and space stepping together with recursive curl estimations. Numerical simulations of an initial-value problem are performed for temporal approximation orders from second to tenth order while the spatial and temporal step sizes are kept fixed. Comparisons with the analytical solution show that the errors decrease rapidly and monotonically with increasing approximation order. These results demonstrate the practical potential of the framework for high-accuracy electromagnetic computation and provide a basis for further development of arbitrary-order numerical methods.

title: Numerical Smoothness and Error Analysis for Evolution Equations
summary: This is a lecture note to introduce the innovative concept of numerical smoothness and its application in the error analysis of numerical solutions of evolution equations. We start from the two fundamentally different error splittings. One splitting is popular, which brings us to local error defined along the original solution and error propagation by numerical schemes. The well know Lax Equivalence Theorem is based on this error splitting. The other splitting can only be seen in a few numerical ODE books, which brings us to local error defined along the numerical solution and error propagation by the solutions of the evolution equations. The innovative concept of numerical smoothness arises from the second error splitting. While there are many difficulties when we use numerical stability in error analysis of nonlinear evolution equations, we will show that numerical smoothness works naturally in error analysis/estimation/control with advantages in several ways. We will define temporal and spatial numerical smoothness indicators, prove the necessity of the boundedness of these indicators for having optimal convergence rate, and show computable error estimates as functions of these smoothness indicators. Moreover, these error estimates are optimal in the approximatons' convergence rates and also optimal in the error propagation of the evolution equation. In comparison with error analysis framework of the Lax Equivalence Theorem, from the necessity results and the error estimates proven in the numerical smoothness framework, we have a new equivalence theory: Consistency + Numerical Smoothness <=> optimal error estimates. Unlike the Lax Equivalence Theorem, the new equivalence theory works well for nonlinear problems, nonlinear schemes, and many other complications of problems.

title: Energy-dependent trapping of backscattered helium during magnetron sputtering growth: A molecular dynamics study
summary: Helium incorporation during magnetron sputtering can strongly affect thin film growth and lead to the formation of gas/solid nanocomposites and nanoporous structures. Here, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are used to investigate the trapping mechanism of helium atoms (He) and the subsequent formation of He bubbles during the sputter deposition of aluminum (Al) and titanium (Ti) thin films. The simulations account for the kinetic energy distributions of sputtered metal atoms and backscattered gas species. Results indicate that He is efficiently incorporated into the growing films, leading to the formation of high-pressure, dense He bubbles, with a much higher He-to-metal atomic ratio in Ti ($\sim$ 60%) than in Al ($\sim$ 12%). More importantly, the simulations reveal a clear energy dependence of He trapping in Ti: background He atoms at thermal energies are essentially not incorporated, whereas efficient trapping starts at an incident energy of approximately 20 eV and increases up to a saturation regime near 100 eV. Simulated thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) further reveals distinct release mechanisms in the two investigated metals: He desorption from Al occurs at higher temperatures and is preceded by the removal of surface Al atoms, whereas He and Ti atom desorption starts continuously around 950 K, leading to a porous structure. Comparative simulations with argon (Ar) demonstrate negligible trapping even at comparable kinetic energy or momentum, showing that neither parameter alone accounts for the strong He incorporation observed in Ti. The above results are in very good agreement with what is reported in literature for low-kinetic energy He ion implantation in metal surfaces, suggesting similar insertion mechanisms. They clarify the atomistic conditions governing noble gas trapping during film growth and provide a basis for controlling He incorporation and porosity in films synthesized by magnetron sputtering.

title: All-electron RT-TDDFT with Exact Exchange based on Numeric Atom-centered Orbitals for Condensed Matter
summary: Real-time time-dependent density functional theory (RT-TDDFT) has become a widely used first-principles method for studying excited-state and nonequilibrium electron dynamics. Hybrid exchange-correlation (XC) functionals, which incorporate a fraction of nonlocal exact exchange, are particularly important for accurately describing processes such as charge transfer and hot-carrier dynamics. However, the high computational cost which accompanies exact exchange, as required in hybrid XC functionals, has largely restricted RT-TDDFT simulations of condensed matter systems to using semi-local XC functionals. In this work, we present an all-electron implementation of exact exchange for RT-TDDFT based on numeric atom-centered orbitals, extending an efficient ground-state resolution-of-identity (RI) framework to the complex, time-dependent Hamiltonians required for real-time propagation. We validate the implementation against an established RI approach, for an isolated water molecule, finding exact agreement for both valence and core (K-edge) excitations. We also demonstrate the method on two extended periodic systems, crystalline silicon and silicon carbide. For silicon, the HSE06 spectrum reproduces previously reported real-time TDDFT results and agrees with experiment to within approximately 0.2~eV, consistent with plane-wave pseudopotential implementations. For silicon carbide, we compute valence and X-ray absorption spectra at the silicon $L$-edge and carbon $K$-edge. These results establish an efficient, all-electron route to hybrid-XC functional RT-TDDFT for both molecular and condensed matter systems.

title: An exact Delaunay flux identity for compact equilibria in the liquid drop model
summary: We revisit the construction of compact liquid drop equilibria from Delaunay unduloids in [Arch. Ration. Mech. Anal. 249 (2025), Paper No. 74]. We evaluate exactly the coefficient arising in the final solvability condition of the Lyapunov-Schmidt reduction, identifying it as the product of the axial period and the normalised Delaunay flux. Using this identity and the monotonicity of the period, we establish the conjectured positivity of the coefficient and prove that its product with the period strictly increases with the neck radius. We also derive an exact relation between the volume and the surface area of one period and prove that both strictly decrease with the neck radius. These results extend the construction throughout the embedded unduloid family and yield compact equilibria of every sufficiently large mass, with reference neck radii converging to any prescribed interior value as the mass tends to infinity.

title: Linear and entropy-stable scheme for the dynamic van der Waals model of non-isothermal liquid-vapor flows
summary: In this paper, we propose a linear and decoupled fully discrete scheme that preserves the entropy production property for the dynamic van der Waals model. This model provides a thermodynamically consistent diffuse-interface framework for describing non-isothermal phase transitions in single-component liquid-vapor systems, containing the coupled conservation laws of mass, momentum and energy. We first introduce an equivalent reformulation of the governing equations that avoids the use of chain-rule identities, which generally fail under discrete differentiation. Further, a component-wise convex-splitting method is employed to calculate the discrete chemical potential and temperature. This treatment provides a discrete entropy-stable inequality without a time step restriction. Based on the explicitly treated velocity, the scheme allows the three conservation equations to be solved linearly and sequentially in a decoupled manner. Since the momentum equation does not directly affect the entropy-stability analysis, we use a classical linear semi-implicit scheme to solve it. Numerical experiments verify the expected numerical accuracy. Simulations of droplet evaporation and two- and three-dimensional Leidenfrost effects further demonstrate the proposed method can capture complex non-isothermal phase-transition dynamics while numerically reproducing the discrete entropy production behavior.

title: Physical-state supervision for design-only Gaussian process surrogates of implosion simulations
comment: 30 pages, 10 figures, 4 tables. Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23253596; code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23255040
summary: Physical diagnostics recorded during simulation can organize a sharply varying response, but using them as surrogate inputs normally requires another calculation at prediction. We construct a physical-state-supervised Gaussian process surrogate that learns these diagnostics from design variables. Cross-fitted state estimates augment a retained design representation; a global Gaussian process and an optional soft mixture of response-band experts use identical inputs. On a database of 1,987 paired one-dimensional implosions, learned burn-weighted states from calculations without alpha-particle heating reduce mean squared log-response error by 60.25% and 52.98% for the global predictor on random holdout and design-space extrapolation. Random-projection and shuffled-state supervision do not reproduce these gains. For CH, matched-input comparisons show that experts help at smaller training budgets but contribute little at 1,000 designs with this representation. A thermal-feedback benchmark validates the complete learned-state procedure, while 3,000 newly calculated Be/Cocktail designs expose weaker extrapolation gains and cases where experts degrade accuracy. A conditional state-error bound separates encoding sensitivity from routing effects. An open Python implementation reproduces the archived predictions and is released with the data, per-design results, and measured costs. Physical-state supervision is thus a useful representation for finite-data surrogates, whereas expert specialization should be selected by validation.

title: Alter-excitons in Altermagnets: Symmetry, Splitting and Dispersion
summary: Magnetism provides a fertile platform for discovering emergent quantum phenomena governed by symmetry. Recent developments of spin-space-group (SSG) theory have revealed altermagnets as a distinct class of nonrelativistic collinear magnets with unconventional spin-dependent electronic structures. Here, we demonstrate that altermagnetic symmetry imposes fundamentally different constraints on electronic and excitonic excitations. Although the quasiparticle and two-body Hamiltonians possess identical SSG symmetries, we find that symmetry-protected degeneracies present in the electronic band structure can be intrinsically lifted in the exciton spectrum at specific momenta. This splitting arises solely from the many-body nature of excitons and does not require spin-orbit coupling or noncollinear magnetic order. Combining symmetry analysis with many-body perturbation theory, we predict a novel class of spin-split excitonic quasiparticles, termed alter-excitons, and reveal their characteristic dispersions in altermagnetic systems. Our results establish excitons as a sensitive probe of hidden spin-space symmetries and uncover a new route toward symmetry-engineered many-body phenomena in collinear magnets.

title: Stability threshold of the Couette flow in 2D Navier-Stokes Boussinesq equations on $\mathbb{T} \times [-1, 1]$ and $\mathbb{R} \times [-1, 1]$
summary:
In this paper, we study the transition threshold problem for the 2D Navier-Stokes Boussinesq equations around the Couette flow with a constant background temperature in two domains: $\mathbb{T} \times [-1, 1]$ and $\mathbb{R} \times [-1, 1]$.
  It was proved that if the sizes of initial perturbations of the vorticity and the temperature in Sobolev spaces are $ν^{\fr13}$ and $ν^{\fr56}$, respectively, then this system admits a globally stable solution.
  Besides, we derive the enhanced dissipation estimate for the vorticity and temperature, as well as the inviscid damping estimate for the velocity. The coupling in the equations poses some difficulties to the analysis. We overcome these challenges and establish the results via the quasi-linear method and energy estimates.

title: Numerical Stability of Extended-Domain Spectral Collocation: Floating-Point Regularization and an Equilibrium Law for the Frame Constants
summary: Extended-domain spectral collocation expands the solution of a boundary value problem in the Laplacian eigenbasis of an enclosing box and collocates at as many nodes as modes. The square system is exponentially ill-conditioned, and the impossibility theorem for equispaced data rules out stable geometric convergence; yet such solvers converge geometrically to a few orders of magnitude above the unit roundoff. We explain why in one dimension. The collocation solution is the solution operator applied to the interpolant of the data in an operator-dependent test space whose Lebesgue constant must grow exponentially for geometric convergence, so exact solutions can amplify data errors exponentially. In floating-point arithmetic the error of any coefficient vector is bounded by its nodal residual, its distance to a competitor and two frame constants, a leakage and a restricted Marcinkiewicz--Zygmund constant, bounded uniformly in the number of modes at a fixed positive threshold; for a backward-stable solve, under a condition on the perturbed matrix, the bound is uniform in the conditioning for suitably analytic data and, with computed constants, within a factor of about ten of the error floor of a direct solver. For the Poisson operator the rate of the two constants along the tail of the spectrum is given by a constrained equilibrium problem of logarithmic potential theory. For an interval of length $L$ extended by $δ$ at each end, the problems for $δ$ and $L^2/(4δ)$ are dual, the rate is linear for $δ= L/2$, and it starts with slope minus the fraction of the extended domain occupied by the extension, so for $δ< L/2$ the leakage constant obeys no power law with the exponent of the end of the spectrum. In experiments, convection--diffusion operators behave like the Poisson operator at moderate Péclet numbers.

title: Precise propagation rates of the fractional Fisher-KPP equation with free boundaries
summary:
In this paper, we determine the propagation rates of the Fisher-KPP equation with free boundaries and fractional diffusion $(-Δ)^s$ $(0<s<1)$, which was considered in \cite{CDN26} as a model for species spreading, where the density function $u(t,x)$ satisfies the fractional Fisher-KPP equation $u_t+(-Δ)^su=f(u)$ over a one-dimensional spatial domain $(g(t), h(t))$, representing the expanding population range, with $x=g(t)$ and $x=h(t)$ the free boundaries. It was shown in \cite{CDN26} that the model is well-posed, and its long-time dynamics exhibits a spreading-vanishing dichotomy. We show in this paper that, when spreading occurs,
  \[ \begin{cases} \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{h(t)}{t^{1/(2s)}} =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{-g(t)}{t^{1/(2s)}} =\left(\frac{2^{1-2s}μ}{1-2s}\right)^{1/(2s)} & \mbox{ if $s\in(0,1/2)$,}\\[2mm] \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{h(t)}{t\ln t} =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{-g(t)}{t\ln t} =μ& \mbox{ if $s=1/2$,}\\[2mm] \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{h(t)}{t} =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{-g(t)}{t} =c_0(s) & \mbox{ if $s\in(1/2,1)$}, \end{cases} \] where $c_0(s)\in (0,\infty)$ is uniquely determined by the associated semi-wave problem. The level sets of $u(t,x)$ propagate with the same rates as the free boundaries. The proof uses delicate upper and lower solutions constructed from a smooth profile function in the case $s\in (0, 1/2]$, and from the semi-wave profile when $s\in (1/2, 1)$.

title: ADER-ZIST - a mixed explicit ADER-DG and zonally implicit space-time DG approach for Cartesian cut cell meshes
summary: We present high order accurate mixed explicit-implicit discontinuous Galerkin (DG) schemes for the solution of hyperbolic systems of conservation laws on Cartesian cut cell meshes. Such meshes may contain arbitrarily small cut cells, which leads to the well-known small cell problem: the CFL condition of explicit schemes would severely restrict the admissible time step. To overcome this difficulty, we use high order explicit fully-discrete one-step ADER-DG schemes only on Cartesian cells away from the embedded boundaries. The zone close to the embedded boundary, which consists of cut cells and their direct face neighbors, is discretized with an implicit space-time DG scheme that is coupled to the explicit scheme directly via the numerical flux. The resulting scheme, called ADER-ZIST (ADER-DG with Zonally Implicit Space-Time DG), is conservative by construction, and its time step is determined only by the size of the Cartesian background cells. Curved embedded boundaries are represented by high order isoparametric sub-triangles inside the cut cells, and the nonlinear system of the implicit cells is solved via an inexact matrix-free Newton-Krylov method. For problems with shock waves, we add an artificial viscosity term whose strength is controlled by an oscillation-eliminating smoothness sensor. ADER-ZIST is assessed on a comprehensive set of test problems for the compressible Euler equations, ranging from smooth flows around straight and curved embedded boundaries to acoustic scattering and shock-dominated flows. The scheme essentially reaches its nominal order of accuracy N+1 for smooth solutions and for polynomial degrees up to N=5, on meshes with minimal volume fractions of the small cut cells down to the order of 10^-7.
